Peter: Let me ask you, Vanessa, have you ever had an accident cooking? I mean have you ever burned anything? Did anything not turn out the way you wanted?
Vanessa: Oh, of course. I used to make a lot of mistakes and burn my food a number of times.
Peter: I find that unbelievable. You're like the perfect chef.

Vanessa: Yeah, I would put in too much of one seasoning. Then my my dishes would taste horrible.
Peter: How did that happen?
Vanessa: If I put in a half ounce of salt instead of a quarter ounce, it alters everything.
Peter: True. I used to cook more often when I was in college. Sometimes when I put in a little less water, it changed the sauce. But I would still eat it.

Vanessa: Yeah, when I was in culinary school, my mom used to help me a lot. We would experiment with how to use various ingredients.
Peter: Nice.
Vanessa: I used to follow recipes very closely, but now I have a sense of how much is enough.

Talking about past habits

"Used to" and "would" express an action that occurred regularly in the past.
You use Wh- questions and yes/no questions to ask about past habits.
You use questions in Present Perfect to ask about experiences.
You use questions in Simple Past to ask about specific facts in the past.

You use used to to talk about the past. It is not a tense but it is like a tense. You use used to for the past only.
You use would to describe the pattern of action in the past.

Structure:
Did anything not turn out the way you wanted?
Was Vanessa always the perfect chef?
Did Peter use to cook a lot?
What did Vanessa's mom used to do?

You use Present Perfect tense to ask about experiences that happened in the past up to now or that are important now.
There is no past time reference.

to burn
to heat or cook a piece of food so much that it becomes brownish black
(verb)
Example: Vanessa used to burn her food a few times.

These are words you use to talk about preparing food.
to turn out
to produce a positive result
(verb)
Example: Sometimes my cooking doesn't turn out the way I want.
engenn6le03ob07aud02
unbelievable
unable to believe something that happened
(adjective)
Example: Peter found it unbelievable that Vanessa ever made any mistakes.
engenn6le03ob07aud03
seasoning
spices put on raw meat before cooking to add flavor
(noun)
Example: Putting on the right amount of seasoning would make your dish taste perfect.
engenn6le03ob07aud04
horrible
really bad
(adjective)
Example: My dish tasted horrible because I put in too much of one seasoning.
engenn6le03ob07aud05
to alter
to change
(verb)
Example: If you put in the wrong ingredients, it could really alter the taste of the dish.
engenn6le03ob07aud06

to try something unknown
(verb)
